n: Interpretation of MCH and MCV in Anemia

faq.a: No; early iron deficiency may have normal MCV, so check ferritin or RDW.
faq.q: Can a normal MCV rule out iron deficiency?

faq.a: RDW measures variation in red cell size; high RDW suggests mixed population, typical of iron deficiency.
Use clinical signs (peripheral neuropathy, glossitis) and response to trial B12 therapy.
faq.q: What if B12 assay is unavailable?

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with heavy menses has Hb 9 g/dL, MCV 72 fL, MCH 22 pg – what is the most likely diagnosis and next investigation? — Iron‑deficiency anaemia; order serum ferritin or iron studies.

A patient on chronic zidovudine presents with Hb 8 g/dL, MCV 110 fL – how does the drug affect the indices and what is the management? — Zidovudine causes macrocytosis; assess for other causes, consider switching if symptomatic, supplement folate.

You receive a peripheral smear showing macro‑ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils; MCV is 115 fL – what deficiency should you suspect and what urgent complication must you prevent? — Vitamin B12 deficiency; prevent irreversible neurological damage.

A child from a malaria‑endemic area has Hb 7 g/dL, MCV 78 fL, normal ferritin – what is the most likely cause and immediate treatment? — Anaemia of chronic disease/malaria; treat malaria and consider iron only if deficiency confirmed.
How does chronic kidney disease alter red cell indices and what adjunct therapy improves anaemia? — Usually normocytic‑normochromic; give erythropoiesis‑stimulating agents when indicated.

A patient with sickle cell disease has a sudden drop in Hb, MCV 85 fL, reticulocyte count 12% – what is the likely event and urgent management? — Acute vaso‑occlusive haemolytic crisis; give analgesia, hydration, consider transfusion.
Why is RDW normal in thalassaemia trait despite low MCV? — Red cells are uniformly small; the size variation is minimal.
In a resource‑limited setting without serum B12, what bedside test can support a diagnosis of B12 deficiency? — Neurological exam for peripheral neuropathy and assessment of tongue (glossitis).
ai.title: Interpretation of MCH and MCV in Anemia
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A systematic approach to anaemia using red cell indices helps narrow differential diagnoses, especially in low‑resource settings. Understand how MCH and MCV guide history‑taking, investigations and management.

b: Low MCV = microcytic; High MCV = macrocytic; Normal MCV = normocytic
sections.p: Anaemia is a common presentation on East African wards. MCH (pg) and MCV (fL) are inexpensive parameters from a full blood count that classify anaemia by red cell size and haemoglobin content.

b: Microcytic‑hypochromic (low MCV, low MCH) → iron deficiency, thalassaemia, chronic infection
Normocytic‑normochromic (normal MCV, normal MCH) → acute blood loss, chronic disease, early renal disease
Macrocytic‑hyperchromic (high MCV, high MCH) → B12/folate deficiency, alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism
sections.p: Combine MCH with MCV to differentiate iron‑deficiency, thalassaemia, chronic disease, B12/folate deficiency, haemolysis and mixed patterns.

b: Ask about menstrual loss, deworming, malaria, HIV, TB, diet low in meat/leafy greens
Examine for pallor, jaundice, splenomegaly, glossitis, neurological signs
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, red cell indices often replace specialised tests. They direct focused history (diet, bleeding, drug exposure) and cheap investigations.
If a test is unavailable, rely on clinical clues and simple bedside tests (e.g., stool occult blood, malaria rapid test, HIV rapid test).

t.b: Provides Hb, RBC, MCV, MCH, RDW – answers what type of anaemia is present
Shows cell size, shape, inclusion bodies – confirms microcytosis, macro‑ovalocytes, schistocytes
Distinguishes iron deficiency from anaemia of chronic disease when MCV is low
Clarifies macrocytic aetiology when MCV is high
Assesses marrow response – high in haemolysis, low in production failure

b: Chronic disease → treat infection (TB, HIV), improve nutrition, consider erythropoietin if renal failure
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; provide supportive care while awaiting results.

b: Thalassaemia trait vs iron deficiency – both microcytic; RDW high in iron deficiency, normal in thalassaemia
Alcoholic macrocytosis vs B12 deficiency – macrocytosis without neurological signs suggests alcohol
sections.p: Other causes of abnormal indices may mimic each other.

b: Acute infection can raise MCV transiently
Severe dehydration concentrates blood, falsely elevating MCH
sections.p: Certain conditions alter indices without true anaemia.

b: Link low MCV + high RDW → iron deficiency; low MCV + normal RDW → thalassaemia
High MCV + neurological signs → B12 deficiency
sections.p: Exam questions often test integration of indices with clinical context.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe dyspnoea, chest pain or syncope with anaemia
New onset neurological deficits (possible B12 deficiency)
Unexplained jaundice with rapid haemoglobin fall
